listenings.text: Okay, note to myself, Thursday night, on the way to the airport. Three days with the Brazilian team, and here is the thing I want to remember for next time. I cannot tell you a single slide from those four presentations. Not one, and I was in all of them. What I can tell you is that the woman from tax spent ten minutes explaining a case she had read about, some poisoning trial from the nineteen twenties, and she was so interested in it that I have already looked it up twice since. And there was a man, I think from treasury, who runs at five in the morning because it is the only hour that belongs to him. Those two I would recognize anywhere. The rest of them spoke in the meetings, and they spoke well, and a week from now I will not be able to give you their names. It has nothing to do with how good their English was. Some of the quietest people in that room had the best English in the building. They just never said anything that was theirs.

There is a study that people in this industry quote all the time and almost nobody has actually read, so here is what it says. Researchers went to four professional conferences and then waited. Six weeks later they went back to the people who had attended and asked them to name everybody they had spoken to. Not the sessions, not the speakers. The people. On average, out of dozens of conversations, participants could name four. And when the researchers looked at those four, the pattern was almost embarrassing in how simple it was. Every single one of them had said something about their life outside work. A daughter learning the violin. A bad knee. A house that was falling apart. It did not matter what it was, and it did not matter whether the other person cared. The ones who had talked only about their job did not disappear exactly, but they came back in the data as a role instead of a person. The auditor from Toronto. The tax guy from Brazil. And more often than not, when the researchers pushed, nobody could remember the name at all.
